questions.q: Does an allowance top-up before a heatwave reduce lost work and medical spending?
questions.have: A Rajshahi delivery simulation was reported. [B5]
questions.could: Randomised phased invitation or top-up timing across comparable neighbourhood clusters, with aggregate income, medical-spending and timing outcomes.
questions.scale: Illustrative design: 40-60 clusters; final size from power calculations.

questions.q: At which access step do heat-exposed urban households stop receiving support?
questions.have: HIES measures past receipt but not a linked eligibility-to-receipt ladder. [B3]
questions.could: A repeated representative household survey linked only to consented, de-identified process totals; publish aggregate transitions and reasons.
questions.scale: Illustrative design: 1,500-2,000 households across several cities.

questions.q: How often does public support meet the costs of medically diagnosed heat illness?
questions.have: A historical SSK financial-risk evaluation exists; heat-specific claims were not reported. [B7]
questions.could: Prospective facility-cost study comparing public benefits, out-of-pocket costs, referral and foregone care across one hot season.
questions.scale: Illustrative design: 10-15 facilities; power and case-volume check first.

questions.q: Does assisted application improve timely receipt among migrants and women outdoor workers?
questions.have: Delivery organisations describe support, but no comparable independent local effect was read. [B6, B12, B13]
questions.could: Randomise outreach timing among consenting community clusters and track aggregate application, receipt, cost and delay.
questions.scale: Illustrative design: 30-50 clusters over one application cycle.

questions.q: When heat arrives, how much of a household's lost earnings and care costs does an allowance or top-up cover, and does it arrive before the hottest days?
questions.have: Implementer reports count households that received cash in Rajshahi and Dhaka. None of the sources checked measures how far the money went, or when it arrived compared with the heat.
questions.could: Follow recipient households through one hot season, recording lost work days, care costs and payment dates against heat-alert dates.
questions.scale: Illustrative: about 300 households in two cities over one hot season

questions.q: How many heat-exposed urban households know of an allowance, qualify for it, hold the documents, apply and are enrolled?
questions.have: None of the sources checked measures these steps for the schemes on this page in Bangladesh.
questions.could: A household survey in hot wards that asks the same people about each step, for the same schemes.
questions.scale: Illustrative: about 1,000 households in four wards

evidence.title: The effectiveness of a government-sponsored health protection scheme in reducing financial risks for the below-poverty-line population in Bangladesh
evidence.finding: KNOWN study estimate: adjusted out-of-pocket expenditure was 33% lower in intervention areas. This is contextual health-financing evidence, not a heat-specific effect.
evidence.limit: Cross-sectional design, recall periods and unmeasured forgone care limit causal interpretation.

evidence.title: Fast Action for Floods: RCT Evidence on Forecast-based Cash Transfers from Bangladesh and Nepal
evidence.scale: Randomised timing of flood-related cash; sample varies across countries and survey rounds
evidence.finding: KNOWN trial findings, with wider transfer to heat INFERRED: earlier cash improved some early food-security and psychosocial outcomes. Later borrowing, savings and asset outcomes did not show statistically significant effects.
evidence.limit: Working paper, not a peer-reviewed heat study; incomplete outcome timing limits some recovery comparisons.

indicators.indicator: Days with daily maximum air temperature above 40 degrees C
indicators.definition: Proposed derivation from hourly ERA5 2 m temperature, using local calendar days and area-weighted aggregation. Threshold is an analytical choice, not an official warning threshold.
indicators.licence: CC-BY licence displayed; retain dataset attribution
indicators.place_code: Grid coordinates; spatial overlay with versioned division geometry
indicators.limit: INFERRED reanalysis; not measured personal exposure. No country values were calculated in this research.

indicators.indicator: Nights with daily minimum air temperature above 30 degrees C
indicators.definition: Proposed derivation from the same hourly series, using local-day minimum as a reproducible proxy. An overnight-only definition can be substituted if documented.
indicators.place_code: Same grid and geometry as hotdays
indicators.limit: INFERRED; a local-day minimum is not a direct measurement of sleep conditions.

indicators.definition: Proposed mean hourly 2 m dew-point temperature for March-June 2025, aggregated by area. This is a humidity context measure, not wet-bulb temperature or WBGT.
indicators.place_code: Same grid and geometry as hotdays
indicators.limit: INFERRED; a humid-heat health threshold has not been validated here. These variables are published on a grid, not as administrative tables.
